```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: true
#| output: false
root <- normalizePath("..")
inputs <- file.path(root, "02.inputs")
outputs <- file.path(root, "03.outputs")
derived <- file.path(inputs, "derived")

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(flextable)
})

# Write figures into the committed outputs folder rather than the render
# sidecar. With embed-resources the sidecar is deleted once its contents are
# inlined into the HTML, which leaves no PNG on disk for the README to show.
# Writing them here keeps a copy that survives the render and is in the
# repository.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.path = file.path("..", "03.outputs", "figures", "mfig-"))
source(file.path(root, "05.scripts", "analysis_functions.R"))

# House table format: 9 pt, centred headers, numeric right, text left, single
# line spacing. Every table goes through fmt_tbl, so the house style is defined
# once and cannot drift between tables.
fmt_tbl <- function(df, right = NULL) {
  right_cols <- union(names(df)[vapply(df, is.numeric, TRUE)], right)
  left_cols <- setdiff(names(df), right_cols)
  ft <- flextable::flextable(df)
  ft <- flextable::fontsize(ft, size = 9, part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::align(ft, align = "center", part = "header")
  if (length(right_cols))
    ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = right_cols, align = "right", part = "body")
  if (length(left_cols))
    ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = left_cols, align = "left", part = "body")
  ft <- flextable::line_spacing(ft, space = 1, part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::padding(ft, padding.top = 1, padding.bottom = 1, part = "all")
  flextable::set_table_properties(ft, layout = "autofit", width = 1)
}

# Read a value out of a two-column item/value table by name. Stops rather than
# returning empty, so a renamed row breaks the render instead of silently
# emptying a sentence.
lookup <- function(tbl, item) {
  v <- tbl$value[tbl$item == item]
  if (length(v) != 1) stop("no unique row for: ", item)
  v
}
n_fmt <- function(x) format(as.numeric(x), big.mark = ",")

# The three series, named once. Everything downstream reads these labels rather
# than repeating them, so the version and the input resolution attached to a
# series cannot drift between a table and the sentence describing it.
SERIES <- c(s1 = "S1: FWI1987, 13:00 observation",
            s2 = "S2: FWI2025, 13:00 observation",
            s3 = "S3: FWI2025, hourly observation")

# The record's extent is read here, before it is described anywhere, so that no
# sentence in this document states a period the data do not cover.
cover <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi-station-season-coverage.csv"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kept <- subset(cover, status == "kept")
n_kept <- nrow(kept)
n_stations_kept <- length(unique(kept$station_name))
yr_first <- min(kept$year); yr_last <- max(kept$year)
n_seasons <- length(unique(kept$year))
```

# Introduction

Fire danger indices are the arithmetic through which fire management sees the
weather. In Canada that arithmetic is the Fire Weather Index System, and it has
been essentially fixed since 1970: six components computed once a day from one
weather observation taken at 13:00 local daylight time, specified by
@vanwagner1987fwi and implemented from the FORTRAN listing of
@vanwagner1985fortran. Almost everything published about how Canadian fire
weather has changed is a statement about that arithmetic. Trends in extreme fire
weather across Canada [@wang2015extreme], the lengthening of the fire season
[@wotton1993seasonlength], the rise in lightning-caused fire risk in Ontario
[@woolford2014lightning], the abrupt increase in British Columbia burning since
the mid-2000s [@parisien2023abrupt] and the drivers of the 2023 Canadian season
[@jain2024canada2023] are all reported in the units of the 1987 system.

In 2025 the Canadian Forest Service Fire Danger Group replaced it. The successor,
which that report labels FWI2025 to keep it distinct from FWI1987
[@cffdg2025fwi2025], is not a recalibration. The first of the key updates its
executive summary lists is "Using hourly weather to better reflect maximum
burning conditions", and section 4.1.1 states that "the time lag function used in
the FWI2025 for the FFMC has been cut in half". The System now runs on an hourly stream,
takes latitude, longitude and date so that daylight length enters the moisture
calculation, and adopts the Initial Spread Index of the Fire Behaviour Prediction
System [@fcfdg1992fbp] in place of the original.

Alongside those changes the report makes a claim of continuity. Section 4.1 says
that "an FFMC of 91 in FWI1987 should correspond to an FFMC of approximately 91
in FWI2025", and that deviations "should reflect meaningful differences in fuel
moisture content". Read as written the claim is about levels, and it is
plausible: the update was designed so that a number on the old scale means
roughly what it used to mean.

The difficulty is that fire danger trends are almost never reported as levels.
They are reported as counts of days above a threshold, as seasonal severity
accumulated over a season, as the frequency of an extreme. Those are properties
of the upper tail, and a change that leaves a distribution's centre alone can
still move its tail. Halving a drying time lag does exactly that kind of thing:
it lets the litter layer respond further within a day, which widens the diurnal
swing without necessarily shifting the daily mean. If it widens the tail, then an
extreme-day count computed under FWI2025 will trend at a different rate from the
same count computed under FWI1987, and every published Canadian fire danger trend
becomes version-contingent in a way that has not been quantified.

Testing that is harder than it looks, because FWI1987 and FWI2025 differ in two
respects at once. FWI1987 takes a single daily observation at 13:00 local
daylight time. FWI2025 "calculations always use hourly weather"
[@cffdg2025fwi2025, section 3.1.1.1] and offers three input pathways, ranked in
that report as best, good and usable: direct hourly observations, daily maxima
and minima, and the legacy 13:00 observation. Running the old system on noon data
against the new system on hourly data therefore confounds the version change with
the input change. A difference found that way could not be attributed to either.

This study separates them. Three danger series are computed from one hourly
weather record for one basin: FWI1987 driven by the 13:00 observation, FWI2025
driven by the same 13:00 observation through the report's pathway C, and FWI2025
driven by the observed hourly weather through pathway A. The first contrast moves
the version and holds the input fixed. The second moves the input and holds the
version fixed. The third is the contrast an agency actually faces when it
migrates, and it is the sum of the other two.

Three questions follow.

**Trend.** What is the `r yr_first` to `r yr_last` trend in seasonal fire danger
in the Okanagan basin under each series, estimated identically?

**Version dependence.** Do the three series give different trends, and if so, is
the difference located in the version or in the input resolution? The prediction
under test is specific and has two ways to fail. Under thresholds fixed in
absolute index units, the faster-drying FWI2025 should widen the upper tail and
produce a steeper positive slope in extreme-day counts than FWI1987. Under
thresholds set as percentiles internal to each series over a common reference
period, that difference should largely vanish, because a percentile threshold
moves with the series it is computed from. Divergence under both schemes, or
under neither, refutes the mechanism rather than supporting it.

**Skill.** Does any of the three predict daily ignition counts better than the
others, and is the relationship between danger and ignition stationary across the
record?

The Okanagan basin is a reasonable place to ask. It is a populated, fire-prone
valley in the southern interior of British Columbia with a long instrumented
record, its fire regime is one where the operational consequences of a migration
decision are expensive, and its terrain is steep enough that a station record is
preferable to a coarse reanalysis. The study detects; it does not attribute.
Nothing here separates a change in fire danger from its causes, and no claim
about anthropogenic forcing is made or implied.

The study area is the `r sa("watershed_group_name")` watershed group of the
British Columbia Freshwater Atlas, `r n_fmt(sa("basin_area_ha"))` ha in the
southern interior of British Columbia, shown in @fig-study-area. Relief runs from
`r n_fmt(sa("dem_min_elev_m"))` m at the valley floor to
`r n_fmt(sa("dem_max_elev_m"))` m on the flanking uplands.

Three official boundaries carry the name Okanagan and they disagree by a factor
of two, so the choice is stated. The provincial major watershed WA2 "Okanagan
River" measures 1,554,467 ha only because it annexes the Similkameen, a separate
valley joined to it in that layer because the Similkameen reaches the Okanogan
River in Washington State rather than because it drains to Okanagan Lake. The
federal Water Survey of Canada sub-sub-drainage 08NM measures 1,203,045 ha
because 402,172 ha of it lies south of the international boundary. Within Canada
the federal and provincial frameworks describe the same basin to within 1.3 per
cent. The study area is therefore the Freshwater Atlas group, the Canadian
portion of the Okanagan watershed, entire. All three boundaries were retrieved
and measured by `05.scripts/resolve_study_area_boundary.R`.

The United States portion of the basin is out of scope by design and not by
oversight. The ignition record is the BC Wildfire Service incident set and the
weather record is the BC Wildfire Service station network, and neither crosses
the border, so a binational basin could not be measured with one consistent
record. Every result below is for the Canadian basin and no inference is offered
about the basin as a whole.

## Two systems

Fire danger here is measured with the Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System,
in both of the versions now in circulation. Because the two are not
interchangeable, every value below carries its version.

**FWI1987** is the System specified by @vanwagner1987fwi. Its six components are
three fuel moisture codes, the Fine Fuel Moisture Code, the Duff Moisture Code
and the Drought Code, and three fire behaviour indices built from them, the
Initial Spread Index, the Buildup Index and the Fire Weather Index. A seventh
quantity, the Daily Severity Rating, is a power transform of the Fire Weather
Index and accumulates over a season into the seasonal severity rating. Its
weather inputs are air temperature, relative humidity, ten-metre open wind speed
and 24 hour rainfall [@lawson2008weather], taken from one observation per day at
13:00 local daylight time. No reference period normalises it: the codes are a
bookkeeping system carried from day to day, so a value depends on the whole
preceding sequence and not only on the day it describes.

**FWI2025** [@cffdg2025fwi2025] keeps those components and changes how they are
computed. The Fine Fuel Moisture Code is calculated hourly, on a modification of
the diurnal method of @vanwagner1977hourly, with the drying time lag halved to
match field observations of litter moisture; under the right conditions it
continues to dry overnight. Canopy interception of the first 0.5 mm of rain
becomes cumulative within a rain event and resets after six rain-free hours
rather than at the end of each day, and the same six hour constant governs the
1.5 mm and 2.8 mm effective rainfall thresholds of the Duff Moisture Code and the
Drought Code. Those two codes are also computed hourly, drying only between
sunrise and sunset, with sunrise and sunset derived from latitude, longitude and
date. The Initial Spread Index takes the Fire Behaviour Prediction System wind
function [@fcfdg1992fbp], which limits the effect of winds above 40 km h^-1^. The
Buildup Index, the Fire Weather Index and the Daily Severity Rating are unchanged
in form.

The optional grassland and peatland components of FWI2025 are excluded. This is a
forest baseline and the two systems are compared only where they overlap.

## Three series

FWI1987 and FWI2025 differ in version and in input resolution simultaneously, so
comparing one against the other answers no question about either. Three series
are computed from a single hourly weather record, and each contrast moves one
thing:

| Series | System | Weather input | Pathway |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | FWI1987 | daily 13:00 LDT observation | the legacy configuration |
| S2 | FWI2025 | daily 13:00 LDT observation | pathway C of @cffdg2025fwi2025 |
| S3 | FWI2025 | observed hourly weather | pathway A of @cffdg2025fwi2025 |

: The three fire danger series and what separates them. {#tbl-design}

@tbl-design is the design. S1 against S2 isolates the version change at fixed
input. S2 against S3 isolates the input resolution change at fixed version. S1
against S3 is the operational contrast an agency faces on migration and is the
sum of the other two. All three run on the same weather, the same season window,
the same startup values and the same gap filling, so nothing that differs between
them is an artefact of the record.

Pathway C is the report's own procedure for the legacy observation. The 13:00
observation is converted to estimated daily maxima and minima using national
constants, daily maximum temperature being about 2 degrees Celsius above the
13:00 value, minimum wind speed 10 per cent of it and maximum wind speed 30 per
cent above it, and humidity carried through at constant vapour content; those
maxima and minima are then expanded to an hourly stream by the sinusoidal method
of @beck1989diurnal with the default offset and decay coefficients of Table A-1
of @cffdg2025fwi2025. Daily rainfall, whose timing is unknown in a once-daily
observation, is placed at the first hour after sunrise, which is the rule the
report gives and the rule FWI1987 implicitly used.

## Weather record

```{r}
#| label: weather-record
#| echo: true
#| output: false
stn_tbl <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "station-metadata.csv"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
```

The weather record is the BC Wildfire Service weather data mart
[@bcws2026datamart], a public directory of hourly observations from the
provincial fire weather station network. It is used in preference to a gridded
reanalysis for two reasons. It carries genuinely hourly precipitation, without
which pathway A cannot be run as specified rather than approximated. And
@cffdg2025fwi2025 states the caveat that a reanalysis would have imposed on this
basin directly: "numerical weather model outputs are not strictly the same as
point observations of weather from a weather station. At the grid cell scale,
outputs from numerical models typically represent what can be thought of as
average conditions across that cell." A cell of roughly nine kilometres across
terrain running from `r n_fmt(sa("dem_min_elev_m"))` m to
`r n_fmt(sa("dem_max_elev_m"))` m is a coarse instrument.

The record retrieved is every hourly observation from the
`r sa("fire_weather_stations")` stations the BC Data Catalogue places inside the
basin polygon, for every season the archive holds. Seasons 1987 to 2023 are
published as one province-wide file per year and seasons 2024 onward as one file
per day; `05.scripts/fetch_fire_weather.py` reads both, streaming each response
and discarding every row outside the basin as it arrives.

Timestamps in that archive are Local Standard Time, which is verified rather than
assumed. The FWI1987 codes that BC Wildfire Service computed operationally appear
in the record at hour 12 and at no other hour. The
standard fire weather observation is 13:00 local daylight time, so hour 12 is
13:00 LDT and the stamp is Pacific Standard Time, UTC-8, year round. The modal
hour of daily maximum temperature in summer falls where that reading implies.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stations
#| tbl-cap: "The weather record. Coverage is the share of the 1 April to 30 September hours in which temperature, humidity and wind were all observed, before any gap filling. A season is kept when coverage reaches 95 per cent and no single gap exceeds 24 hours."
#| echo: true
tz <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "timezone-verification.csv"))

agg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cover, cover$station_name), function(d) {
  k <- subset(d, status == "kept")
  data.frame(
    Station = d$station_name[1],
    `Elevation (m)` = round(d$elevation_m[1]),
    `First season` = ifelse(nrow(k), min(k$year), NA),
    `Last season` = ifelse(nrow(k), max(k$year), NA),
    `Seasons kept` = nrow(k),
    `Seasons dropped` = sum(d$status == "dropped, coverage"),
    `Not reporting` = sum(d$status == "station not reporting"),
    `Median coverage` = round(median(k$observed_fraction), 3),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
agg <- agg[order(-agg$`Seasons kept`), ]
fmt_tbl(agg)
```

@tbl-stations gives the result. `r n_kept` station-seasons across
`r n_stations_kept` stations survive, spanning `r yr_first` to `r yr_last`,
`r n_seasons` distinct seasons. The daily codes appear at hour 12 in
`r n_fmt(tz$daily_codes_at_hour_12)` records and at other hours in
`r tz$daily_codes_at_other_hours`, which is what fixes the convention. The modal
hour of daily maximum temperature in summer is
`r tz$modal_hour_of_max_temp_summer`:00 Local Standard Time, three hours after
solar noon at this longitude, which is consistent with it.

### Season window

The window is a fixed calendar one, 1 May to 30 September, 153 days, with the
calculation spun up from 1 April so that thirty days of weather precede the first
reported day.

That is a departure from the framing of this study, which proposed the Canadian
rule that section C-2.3 of @cffdg2025fwi2025 describes as the criterion most often
used across Canada, to "start calculation three days after the disappearance of
snow cover", or, where snow cover cannot be observed, after three days above 12
degrees Celsius [@lawson2008weather]. The rule was implemented, run, and
abandoned. These stations do not report through the winter, and the rule fired on
whatever day a station was switched on. It produced a season of three days at
Brenda Mines in 1991 and 244 days at Fintry in 1999. Those two figures are the
only numbers in this document not computed by it: they come from the run that
rejected the rule, are recorded in the project's framing document, and cannot be
recomputed here because the procedure that produced them is no longer in the code.
They describe field operations, not climate.

One consequence is stated rather than repaired. **Fire season length cannot be
estimated from this network** and is therefore not among the metrics, although
lengthening season is among the most-reported fire danger trends
[@wotton1993seasonlength]. A network whose stations are switched on and off for
operational reasons cannot measure when a season begins. The metrics that remain
are counts and sums over a window of fixed length, which the network can measure.

### Gaps and startup

Runs of missing temperature, humidity or wind up to 24 hours are filled by linear
interpolation, since the reference implementation requires a gap-free hourly
stream. Missing precipitation is filled with zero, because rain cannot be
invented. A station-season is kept only where at least 95 per cent of the 1 April
to 30 September hours were observed and no single gap exceeded 24 hours.

Filling a gap with no rain makes a missing wet spell look dry and pushes danger
up. The direction matters and is stated: coverage in this record is worse early
than late, so this bias, where it acts, inflates danger in early seasons and
therefore works against an increasing trend rather than for one. It is identical
across the three series by construction, since all three run on the same filled
record, and so cannot move a contrast between versions.

Each station-season starts from FFMC 85, DMC 6 and DC 15, the values
@vanwagner1987fwi gives and the reference implementation defaults to. The Drought
Code is not overwintered, because these stations report no winter weather for an
overwintering calculation to run on. The Drought Code therefore carries startup
information into early May in every season, identically in all three series.

## Implementation

FWI2025 is computed with the reference implementation published by the Canadian
Forest Service Fire Danger Group [@nrcan2026cffdrsng], vendored into this
repository at the commit named in the bibliography and run unmodified. It
reproduces the standard output distributed with it exactly, to the last decimal
place the file carries, over the 2,623 hour Petawawa Research Forest test record.

FWI1987 is implemented for this study in `05.scripts/fwi1987.py`, because both
systems had to run inside one process on one record. Code written for a study is
not evidence, so it is checked twice and both checks are reported in the results
rather than asserted here. The first check is against the CRAN package `cffdrs`
[@wang2017cffdrs], an independently published implementation maintained by the
Canadian Forest Service, run through R over the same test record. The second is
against the FWI1987 codes that BC Wildfire Service itself computed operationally
at these stations at the time, which the data mart preserves alongside the raw
observations: a different party, different code, different decade, and the same
weather.

Two constants differ between @vanwagner1987fwi as printed and
@vanwagner1985fortran as programmed, and this implementation follows the program.
The moisture transform coefficient is 147.2772, not the rounded 147.2 of the
report, since 59.5 x 250 / 101 = 147.27722772 is the value that closes the scale;
and the Duff Moisture Code moisture functions take the listing's form. Using the
rounded constants instead moves the Fine Fuel Moisture Code by up to 3.9 units
over the test record, which would have entered a version comparison as a
difference between systems when it is a difference between roundings.

### Quotation checking

Every passage this document places inside quotation marks and attributes to
@cffdg2025fwi2025 is checked against the report itself by
`05.scripts/verify_quotations.py`, which opens the PDF, repairs hyphenation broken
across lines, collapses whitespace and searches for the exact string, case
included. The check writes `02.inputs/derived/quotation-verification.csv` with the
page each quotation was found on, and exits non-zero if any fails. It found one
failure on its first run, a lower-cased initial letter in the executive summary
quotation above, which is the class of error it exists to catch.

## Fire activity

```{r}
#| label: ignition-inputs
#| echo: true
#| output: false
ign_daily <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "ignitions-daily.csv"),
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ign_daily$date <- as.Date(ign_daily$date)
completeness <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "ignition-completeness.csv"),
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
attribution <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "ignition-attribution.csv"),
                        stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

n_total_incidents <- sum(completeness$n_incidents)
n_dated <- sum(completeness$n_dated)
n_undated <- n_total_incidents - n_dated
pct_dated <- round(100 * n_dated / n_total_incidents, 1)

# Dating completeness by decade, computed here so the sentence below quotes the
# table rather than describing it from memory.
completeness$decade <- paste0(completeness$year %/% 10 * 10, "s")
cd_pre <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(completeness, completeness$decade), function(d)
  data.frame(decade = d$decade[1],
             pct_dated = 100 * sum(d$n_dated) / sum(d$n_incidents))))
cd_pre <- cd_pre[order(cd_pre$decade), ]
```

The ignition record is the BC Wildfire Service historical incident set
[@bcws2026incidents], clipped to the basin: `r n_fmt(n_total_incidents)`
incidents over the `r sa("first_year")` to `r sa("last_year")` seasons.

Two properties of that record govern what can be asked of it, and neither is
repaired here, because neither can be.

**Many incidents cannot be placed on a day at all.** `r n_fmt(n_dated)` of
`r n_fmt(n_total_incidents)` incidents, `r pct_dated` per cent, carry an ignition
date; the remaining `r n_fmt(n_undated)` cannot enter a daily series at any
threshold. The missing dates are not spread evenly, and they do not concentrate
where intuition puts them. The earliest decade in the record is
`r round(head(cd_pre$pct_dated, 1), 0)` per cent dated and the most recent is
`r round(tail(cd_pre$pct_dated, 1), 0)` per cent. Missing date and missing cause
are largely the same records.

**Cause attribution is not stationary.** @tbl-completeness gives both by decade.
A lightning-caused count that falls after 2000 may be recording a change in how
cause was coded rather than a change in ignition.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-completeness
#| tbl-cap: "Completeness of the ignition record by decade. A dated incident can be placed on a day; an attributed incident carries a recorded cause. Both fall sharply after 2000 and the same records are usually missing both."
#| echo: true
completeness$decade <- paste0(completeness$year %/% 10 * 10, "s")
cd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(completeness, completeness$decade), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Decade = d$decade[1],
    Incidents = sum(d$n_incidents),
    Dated = sum(d$n_dated),
    `Dated %` = round(100 * sum(d$n_dated) / sum(d$n_incidents), 1),
    Attributed = sum(d$n_caused),
    `Attributed %` = round(100 * sum(d$n_caused) / sum(d$n_incidents), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
fmt_tbl(cd)
```

The design responds to both rather than caveating them. The ignition models below
carry season as a fixed effect, so the danger coefficient is identified only from
day-to-day variation inside a season. Reporting completeness and cause coding
both change between seasons and neither changes within one, so a between-season
contrast would confound the danger effect with the record keeping and a
within-season contrast cannot. Three response series are modelled, lightning,
person-caused and all causes together, because the all-cause series cannot be
affected by cause coding at all and is therefore the one that carries the weight
when the three disagree. And because detection of small fires also improved over
the record, every result is reported at three minimum sizes, no limit, one
hectare and four hectares. A conclusion that survives at only one threshold is
reported as not surviving.

## Analysis

### Seasonal metrics

Six seasonal metrics are computed per station, season and series over the 1 May
to 30 September window: mean Fire Weather Index, seasonal severity rating as the
sum of the Daily Severity Rating, peak Buildup Index, and counts of days above
each of three thresholding schemes described next. Because FWI2025 produces an
hourly value and FWI1987 a daily one, the FWI2025 series are summarised to a
daily value at 16:00 Local Standard Time, which is 17:00 local daylight time. That
hour is the conventional peak burn hour, and it is the modal hour of peak burning
conditions in the reference implementation's own distributed output. It is not
chosen from this record; for comparison, the modal hour of daily maximum summer
temperature here is `r tz$modal_hour_of_max_temp_summer`:00 Local Standard Time.
The daily maximum over all 24 hours is carried as a sensitivity and is not the
primary, because the maximum of 24 draws exceeds a single daily value for reasons
that have nothing to do with the version change.

### Thresholds

The second question lives in the thresholding, so both schemes are built and
neither is preferred.

*Absolute* thresholds are fixed numbers on the index scale applied unchanged to
all three series, which is the scheme an agency uses, because a danger class is a
number in a manual. Three are used. FFMC 91 is taken from section 4.1 of
@cffdg2025fwi2025, so that counting days above it tests that report's
comparability sentence directly. Fire Weather Index 19 and 30 are the Canadian
high and extreme class boundaries in common use.

*Relative* thresholds are percentiles of each series' own distribution over a
common reference period, taken as 1991 to 2020, the current World Meteorological
Organization normal, and fixed before any metric was computed. A day above a
series' own 90th percentile means the same thing in each series by construction,
so a difference in trend under relative thresholds cannot be an artefact of the
two systems sitting at different levels.

One property of that construction has to be said plainly, because it looks like a
result and is not: inside the reference period the mean number of days above a
series' own 90th percentile is ten per cent of the days in it, in every series, by
definition. The level of a relative count therefore carries no information about
the version at all, and only its trend does.

Reference distributions are computed per station as well as per series. Pooling
them would mix a valley station at
`r round(min(stn_tbl$ELEVATION))` m with a ridge station at
`r n_fmt(round(max(stn_tbl$ELEVATION)))` m, and the percentile would then describe
the network rather than the site.

### Trend estimation

Trends are estimated over the `r n_seasons` seasons from `r yr_first` to
`r yr_last` that survive the coverage rule, with the Theil-Sen
slope, the median of all pairwise slopes [@sen1968slope], computed on the actual
season numbers so that a gap in the sequence is honoured rather than treated as a
step of one. The Theil-Sen estimator is used in preference to least squares
because seasonal counts of extreme days are skewed and a least squares slope on
them is pulled by single seasons.

Significance is the Mann-Kendall test [@mann1945nonparametric] with the
@hamed1998mmk variance correction, which inflates the variance of the test
statistic by the serial correlation actually present in the series rather than
assuming independence. Serial correlation in seasonal fire danger is real, and an
uncorrected Mann-Kendall over-rejects in its presence; the uncorrected result is
reported alongside only to show the size of that effect. Prewhitening
[@yue2002prewhitening] is not used, because it removes part of the trend it is
meant to test for.

One approximation in that correction is stated rather than buried. Coverage drops
seasons out of the middle of some station records, so the season sequence is not
evenly spaced. The Mann-Kendall statistic itself is unaffected, because it depends
on the order of the values and not on their spacing, and the Theil-Sen slope is
computed on the actual season numbers so a gap is a gap. The Hamed and Rao
variance correction, however, estimates autocorrelation at lags counted in
observations rather than in years, which across a gap compares seasons further
apart than the lag says. The direction of that error is knowable: it attributes to
lag one a correlation measured over two or more years, which is smaller, so the
correction applied is smaller than the true one and the test is less conservative
than it would be on a complete record. This is a reason to read a marginal result
here as weaker than its q value suggests, not stronger.

Metric families are corrected within each series by the @benjamini1995fdr false
discovery rate procedure. Confidence intervals on a single slope are bootstrap
percentile intervals over 2,000 resamples of seasons.

### Slope differences

The three series come from one weather record and are therefore strongly
dependent, so a two-sample comparison of their slopes would be wrong. The
difference between two series' slopes is estimated by resampling whole seasons
with replacement and recomputing both slopes on the same resampled seasons in
every one of 4,000 replicates. The pairing is preserved by construction, so the
interval is on the difference and not on two separately noisy slopes. A two-sided
bootstrap p value is taken as twice the smaller tail mass either side of zero, and
is corrected for false discovery rate within the eight metrics of one contrast at
one station.

### Ignition models

Daily ignition counts are modelled as negative binomial with a log link. The
linear predictor carries the daily basin danger value, two annual harmonics in
day of year, season as a factor, and the number of stations that contributed to
the basin mean that day, since no station reports in every season and the
composition of the network changes. That last term cannot affect the comparison
between series in any case, because all three are averaged over exactly the same
stations on exactly the same days. Predictive skill is compared by leaving one
season out at a time, refitting without it, and scoring the held-out season by
its log likelihood under the refitted model. Comparing series on held-out
likelihood rather than on in-sample fit is the point: three series computed from
one weather record will all fit, and the question is which predicts.

### Detectability

What a window of `r n_seasons` seasons cannot resolve is computed rather than
hedged. For
each metric the minimum detectable trend is the slope at which a two-sided test
at alpha 0.05 would reach 80 per cent power given the residual spread of that
metric about its own Theil-Sen line, adjusted for the efficiency of the Theil-Sen
estimator relative to least squares. A null result is reported against that
number, so that "no trend detected" is separated from "no trend".

### Status of claims

Everything below is exploratory and none of it is pre-registered. The project this
manuscript belongs to runs a gated pipeline in which a framing document, a prior
work survey, an analysis design and a pre-registration each close before the next
opens, and outcome data are not touched until the last of those is fixed in
writing. Those gates were deliberately overridden to produce this draft in one
pass.

The consequence is specific and is not a formality. Several decisions that a
pre-registration would have fixed in advance were instead made while the data were
in view: the season window, after the weather-derived rule failed; the coverage
threshold; the reference period; the daily summary hour. Each is stated where it
was made and each is defensible on its own terms, but a decision made in sight of
the data is not the same as a decision made before it, and no p value here should
be read as though it were. What the design does protect is the comparison between
series, because all three run on the same record through the same decisions, so a
choice that moves one moves all three.
