## Implementation checks

```{r}
#| label: tbl-verify
#| tbl-cap: "Verification of the FWI1987 implementation. The first block compares it against the CRAN package cffdrs over the Petawawa Research Forest test record. The second compares it against the FWI1987 codes BC Wildfire Service computed operationally at these stations, pooled over all kept station-seasons."
#| echo: true
val <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi1987-validation.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
opc <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "fwi1987-operational-check.csv"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# The two blocks differ by ten orders of magnitude, so the differences are
# formatted as strings rather than left to the table's numeric printing, which
# would render machine epsilon as a wall of zeros.
fmt_diff <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", formatC(x, format = "g", digits = 3))

blk1 <- data.frame(
  Check = "against cffdrs",
  Component = val$component,
  n = format(val$n, big.mark = ","),
  `Max absolute difference` = fmt_diff(val$max_abs_diff),
  `Mean absolute difference` = fmt_diff(val$mean_abs_diff),
  `Correlation` = "",
  check.names = FALSE)

# The data mart names the operational columns in full; the initials are the
# component names used everywhere else in this document.
initials <- function(x) vapply(strsplit(x, "_"),
                               function(p) paste0(substr(p, 1, 1), collapse = ""),
                               character(1))
op_agg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(opc, opc$component), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Check = "against operational codes",
    Component = initials(d$component[1]),
    n = format(sum(d$n), big.mark = ","),
    `Max absolute difference` = "",
    `Mean absolute difference` = fmt_diff(weighted.mean(abs(d$mean_bias), d$n)),
    `Correlation` = formatC(weighted.mean(d$pearson_r, d$n), format = "f", digits = 4),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
rownames(op_agg) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(rbind(blk1, op_agg))
```

```{r}
#| label: verify-prose
#| echo: true
#| output: false
max_cffdrs <- max(val$max_abs_diff)
op_r <- weighted.mean(opc$pearson_r, opc$n)
op_n <- sum(opc$n)
bias_of <- function(comp) {
  d <- opc[opc$component == comp, ]
  weighted.mean(abs(d$mean_bias), d$n)
}
r_of <- function(comp) {
  d <- opc[opc$component == comp, ]
  weighted.mean(d$pearson_r, d$n)
}
dc_bias <- bias_of("DROUGHT_CODE")
bui_bias <- bias_of("BUILDUP_INDEX")
ffmc_r <- r_of("FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE")
```

@tbl-verify gives both checks. Against `cffdrs` the two implementations agree to
`r formatC(max_cffdrs, format = "g", digits = 2)` across all seven components,
which is machine precision: they are the same arithmetic, and the check confirms
that the equations were transcribed correctly rather than that they are correct.

Against the operational codes, computed by a different party in a different
decade, the weighted mean correlation over `r n_fmt(op_n)` station-days is
`r round(op_r, 3)`. That check is not expected to be exact, and one of its
disagreements is large and has a known cause. The mean absolute bias in the
Drought Code is `r round(dc_bias, 0)` units, and in the Buildup Index, which is
computed from it, `r round(bui_bias, 1)`. BC Wildfire Service overwinters the
Drought Code, carrying it from the previous autumn; this study restarts it at 15
on 1 April, because these stations report no winter weather for an overwintering
calculation to use. That is a difference in convention, not an error, and its
direction is known: a restarted Drought Code is lower than an overwintered one.
Every absolute Drought Code and Buildup Index level reported here is conditional
on that convention. It cannot affect any comparison between the three series,
because all three restart identically.

The components that do not depend on the overwintered code agree closely. The
Fine Fuel Moisture Code correlates
`r round(opc$pearson_r[opc$component == "FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE"] |> weighted.mean(opc$n[opc$component == "FINE_FUEL_MOISTURE_CODE"]), 4)`
with the operational value, which is the component the version comparison
principally rests on.

## Where thresholds fall

```{r}
#| label: tbl-thresholds
#| tbl-cap: "Where each absolute threshold falls in each series' own 1991 to 2020 reference distribution, averaged over stations. A threshold at the same percentile in every series would mean the three systems are interchangeable for counting extremes. The reference median is the median of that component over the same distribution."
#| echo: true
tp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(thresh_pct, list(thresh_pct$series, thresh_pct$component,
                         thresh_pct$threshold), drop = TRUE),
  function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    Component = toupper(d$component[1]),
    Threshold = d$threshold[1],
    `Percentile of threshold` = round(mean(d$percentile_of_threshold, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days per season above` = NA_real_,
    `Reference median` = round(mean(d$reference_median, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
# Days per season above each absolute threshold, averaged over station-seasons.
days_above <- function(series, component, thr) {
  col <- switch(paste(component, thr),
                "ffmc 91" = "n_ffmc_ge91",
                "fwi 19" = "n_fwi_ge19",
                "fwi 30" = "n_fwi_ge30")
  mean(metrics[[col]][metrics$series == series], na.rm = TRUE)
}
key <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(rownames(tp), "\\."))
tp$`Days per season above` <- round(mapply(days_above, key[, 1], key[, 2],
                                           as.numeric(key[, 3])), 1)
tp <- tp[order(tp$Component, tp$Threshold, tp$Series), ]
rownames(tp) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(tp)
```

```{r}
#| label: threshold-prose
#| echo: true
#| output: false
ffmc91 <- subset(tp, Component == "FFMC" & Threshold == 91)
fwi19 <- subset(tp, Component == "FWI" & Threshold == 19)
p_s1 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S1", ffmc91$Series)]
p_s2 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S2", ffmc91$Series)]
p_s3 <- ffmc91$`Percentile of threshold`[grepl("S3", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s1 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S1", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s2 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S2", ffmc91$Series)]
d_s3 <- ffmc91$`Days per season above`[grepl("S3", ffmc91$Series)]
```

@tbl-thresholds tests the comparability sentence of @cffdg2025fwi2025 directly.
A Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91 sits at the `r p_s1`th percentile of the S1
distribution, the `r p_s2`th of S2 and the `r p_s3`th of S3. In days per season
above it, that is `r d_s1` under S1, `r d_s2` under S2 and `r d_s3` under S3.

```{r}
#| label: threshold-reading
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The comparability claim is about where a value sits, so the reading is stated
# in the two units that matter and neither is rounded away: the percentile spread
# across series, and the difference in days per season an agency would count.
pct_spread <- max(abs(p_s3 - p_s1), abs(p_s2 - p_s1))
day_gap <- d_s3 - d_s1
day_gap_pct <- 100 * day_gap / d_s1
```

The claim survives as a statement about levels and does not survive as a statement
about counts. The three medians of the Fine Fuel Moisture Code over the reference
period sit within about a unit of each other, so a value of 91 does mean much what
it used to mean. But the same threshold selects `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(day_gap))`
`r if (day_gap >= 0) "more" else "fewer"` days per season under S3 than under S1,
a difference of `r sprintf("%.0f", abs(day_gap_pct))` per cent, because the
percentile it occupies moves by `r sprintf("%.1f", pct_spread)` points. Those are
the same distributions, described two ways. @fig-distributions shows why: the
curves sit almost on top of one another through the middle and separate where the
threshold is.

```{r}
#| label: fig-distributions
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the daily Fine Fuel Moisture Code and the daily Fire Weather Index over all kept station-days under the three series, with the absolute thresholds marked. The comparability claim of the 2025 report concerns the position of a value on the scale; an extreme-day count concerns the mass beyond a threshold, which is a different quantity."
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0), cex = 0.75)
cols <- c(s1 = "#1B4F72", s2 = "#B7950B", s3 = "#943126")

plot_dens <- function(cols_prefix, xlab, cuts, xlim) {
  dens <- lapply(names(cols), function(s) {
    v <- series_daily[[paste0(s, "_", cols_prefix)]]
    density(v[is.finite(v)], na.rm = TRUE)
  })
  ymax <- max(vapply(dens, function(d) max(d$y), numeric(1)))
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = c(0, ymax * 1.05), xlab = xlab,
       ylab = "Density", main = "")
  for (i in seq_along(dens)) lines(dens[[i]], col = cols[i], lwd = 1.8)
  abline(v = cuts, lty = 3, col = "grey30")
  legend("topleft", legend = unname(SERIES), col = cols, lwd = 1.8, bty = "n",
         cex = 0.72)
}
plot_dens("ffmc", "Fine Fuel Moisture Code", 91, c(40, 101))
plot_dens("fwi", "Fire Weather Index", c(19, 30), c(0, 60))
par(op)
```

## The mechanism

```{r}
#| label: fig-mechanism
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Ten days of the hourly Fine Fuel Moisture Code at Penticton RS in August 2003, under FWI2025 driven by the observed hourly weather and under FWI2025 driven by the 13:00 observation alone. Both are the same system on the same days; the only difference is what the System was told about the weather. The vertical lines mark 13:00 local daylight time, the hour FWI1987 observes, and 17:00, the hour a daily value conventionally represents."
ex <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "example-season-hourly.csv"),
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ex$t <- as.POSIXct(sprintf("%04d-%02d-%02d %02d:00:00", ex$yr, ex$mon, ex$day, ex$hr),
                   tz = "UTC")
win <- ex[ex$mon == 8 & ex$day >= 14 & ex$day <= 23, ]

op <- par(mar = c(3.2, 4, 1.2, 1), cex = 0.8)
plot(win$t, win$s3_ffmc, type = "l", col = cols["s3"], lwd = 1.6,
     ylim = range(c(win$s3_ffmc, win$s2_ffmc), na.rm = TRUE),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Fine Fuel Moisture Code", xaxt = "n")
lines(win$t, win$s2_ffmc, col = cols["s2"], lwd = 1.6)
axis.POSIXct(1, win$t, format = "%d %b")
# The hour markers are drawn thin and pale on purpose: they locate the two
# sampling hours without competing with the curves, which are the subject.
abline(v = win$t[win$hr == 12], col = "grey86", lty = 3, lwd = 0.6)
abline(v = win$t[win$hr == 16], col = "grey62", lty = 2, lwd = 0.6)
lines(win$t, win$s3_ffmc, col = cols["s3"], lwd = 1.6)
lines(win$t, win$s2_ffmc, col = cols["s2"], lwd = 1.6)
legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.75,
       legend = c(unname(SERIES[c("s3", "s2")]),
                  "13:00 LDT, the FWI1987 observation", "17:00 LDT"),
       col = c(cols["s3"], cols["s2"], "grey86", "grey62"),
       lwd = c(1.6, 1.6, 0.8, 0.8), lty = c(1, 1, 3, 2))
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-capability
#| tbl-cap: "Two quantities FWI2025 reports and FWI1987 cannot: the hour at which peak burning conditions occur, and the number of hours per day the burning window stays open, both as the specification's own daily summary computes them. Values are means over kept station-seasons. FWI1987 has no entry because a system with one value per day cannot say when in the day it applies."
#| echo: true
cap <- metrics[metrics$series %in% c("s2", "s3") &
                 !is.na(metrics$mean_peak_hr), ]
if (nrow(cap)) {
  ct <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(cap, cap$series), function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    `Mean peak hour (LST)` = round(mean(d$mean_peak_hr, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Mean burning window (h)` = round(mean(d$mean_duration, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    `Days per season with window >= 6 h` = round(mean(d$n_duration_ge6, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
  rownames(ct) <- NULL
  fmt_tbl(ct)
} else {
  fmt_tbl(data.frame(Note = "Daily summaries were not produced for this run."))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: mechanism-reading
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The two readings the figure supports, computed from the same window it draws.
night <- win$hr %in% c(2, 3, 4, 5)
day <- win$hr %in% c(14, 15, 16, 17)
night_gap <- mean(win$s3_ffmc[night] - win$s2_ffmc[night], na.rm = TRUE)
day_gap <- mean(win$s3_ffmc[day] - win$s2_ffmc[day], na.rm = TRUE)
range_s3 <- mean(tapply(win$s3_ffmc, win$day, function(v) diff(range(v))))
range_s2 <- mean(tapply(win$s2_ffmc, win$day, function(v) diff(range(v))))
```

@fig-mechanism shows what separates S2 from S3 on the same ten days. Both are
FWI2025, both are given the same rain, and the only difference is whether the
System was handed the observed hourly weather or asked to reconstruct a standard
diurnal curve from the 13:00 observation.

The reconstruction is not a smoothed version of the observation; it is a different
shape. Over these days it swings `r sprintf("%.1f", range_s2)` code units between
its daily minimum and maximum against `r sprintf("%.1f", range_s3)` for the
observed series, and the difference is concentrated overnight: the two run
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(day_gap))` units apart in the mid-afternoon and
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(night_gap))` units apart before dawn. A standard curve
anchored to one afternoon reading has to guess the night, and it guesses wetter
than the nights actually were. @tbl-capability gives the consequence in the two
quantities only the hourly system produces at all.

## Trends

```{r}
#| label: trend-compute
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The metric family. Each entry is a column of the seasonal metric table, a
# label, and which thresholding scheme it belongs to. The family is declared
# here, once, and the false discovery rate correction is applied within it.
METRICS <- data.frame(
  col = c("mean_fwi", "ssr", "peak_bui",
          "n_ffmc_ge91", "n_fwi_ge19", "n_fwi_ge30",
          "n_fwi_p90", "n_fwi_p95"),
  label = c("Mean FWI", "Seasonal severity rating", "Peak BUI",
            "Days FFMC >= 91", "Days FWI >= 19", "Days FWI >= 30",
            "Days above own 90th percentile", "Days above own 95th percentile"),
  scheme = c("level", "level", "level",
             "absolute", "absolute", "absolute",
             "relative", "relative"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Trends are estimated per station and per series, then combined, rather than on
# a basin average, because the set of reporting stations changes between seasons
# and a basin average would move when a station joins or leaves.
trend_rows <- list()
for (s in names(SERIES)) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(METRICS))) {
    m <- METRICS$col[i]
    for (stn in unique(metrics$station_name)) {
      d <- metrics[metrics$series == s & metrics$station_name == stn, ]
      d <- d[is.finite(d[[m]]), ]
      if (nrow(d) < 15) next
      tt <- trend_test(d$year, d[[m]])
      tt$series <- s; tt$metric <- m; tt$station <- stn
      tt$mdt <- minimum_detectable_trend(d$year, d[[m]])
      trend_rows[[length(trend_rows) + 1]] <- tt
    }
  }
}
trends <- do.call(rbind, trend_rows)
if (is.null(trends) || !nrow(trends))
  stop("No station has the 15 seasons the trend estimator requires. ",
       "Kept station-seasons: ", n_kept, " over ", n_seasons, " seasons. ",
       "Re-run 05.scripts/fetch_fire_weather.py and ",
       "05.scripts/compute_fwi_series.py over the full archive.")
# The family is the eight metrics within one series at one station.
trends$q <- ave(trends$p_corrected,
                paste(trends$series, trends$station), FUN = fdr)
write.csv(trends, file.path(outputs, "trend-estimates.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trends
#| tbl-cap: "Theil-Sen slopes per season for each seasonal metric under each series, pooled across stations as the median station slope, with the range across stations. Significance is Mann-Kendall with the Hamed and Rao variance correction; the count is of stations at which the false discovery rate adjusted p value falls below 0.05 within that station's eight-metric family. The minimum detectable trend is the slope this record could resolve at 80 per cent power."
#| echo: true
tr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trends, list(trends$series, trends$metric),
                                  drop = TRUE), function(d) {
  data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
    Stations = nrow(d),
    `Median slope` = round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    `Slope range` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", min(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE),
                            max(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE)),
    `Stations q < 0.05` = sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Min detectable` = round(median(d$mdt, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
tr <- tr[order(match(tr$Metric, METRICS$label), tr$Series), ]
rownames(tr) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(tr)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-trends
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 7.0
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Seasonal metrics by season under the three series, pooled across stations as the station mean, with the Theil-Sen line for each series. The absolute and relative extreme-day counts are the panels the second question turns on: the prediction is that the absolute counts separate between series and the relative counts do not."
show <- c("mean_fwi", "ssr", "n_ffmc_ge91", "n_fwi_ge19", "n_fwi_p90", "n_fwi_p95")
# Generous bottom margin and tightened axis title placement: at three rows on one
# page the default margin clips the x axis label against the panel below.
op <- par(mfrow = c(3, 2), mar = c(3.8, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0),
          cex = 0.68)
for (m in show) {
  ylab <- METRICS$label[match(m, METRICS$col)]
  rng <- range(metrics[[m]], na.rm = TRUE)
  plot(NA, xlim = range(metrics$year), ylim = rng, xlab = "Season", ylab = ylab,
       main = "")
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    d <- metrics[metrics$series == s, ]
    a <- aggregate(d[[m]], list(year = d$year), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
    points(a$year, a$x, col = cols[s], pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
    sl <- theil_sen(a$year, a$x)
    ic <- median(a$x - sl * a$year)
    abline(a = ic, b = sl, col = cols[s], lwd = 1.6)
  }
  if (m == show[1])
    legend("topleft", legend = unname(SERIES), col = cols, lwd = 1.6, bty = "n",
           cex = 0.7)
}
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: trend-reading
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The direction and strength of the trend picture, computed rather than eyeballed
# off the table, so the sentence below cannot say something the numbers do not.
tr_up <- sum(trends$slope > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
tr_n <- sum(is.finite(trends$slope))
tr_sig <- sum(trends$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
tr_sig_up <- sum(trends$q < 0.05 & trends$slope > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
# What the autocorrelation correction cost, in tests that would otherwise pass.
would_pass <- sum(p.adjust(trends$p_uncorrected, "BH") < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
infl <- median(trends$n_over_nstar, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Of the `r tr_n` station, series and metric combinations in @tbl-trends,
`r tr_up` have a positive Theil-Sen slope. After the Hamed and Rao correction for
serial correlation and the false discovery rate correction within each station's
eight-metric family, `r tr_sig` remain below a q value of 0.05, `r tr_sig_up` of
them positive. The serial correlation correction is not decorative: the median
ratio of nominal to effective sample size is `r sprintf("%.2f", infl)`, and
`r would_pass` combinations would have passed the same false discovery threshold
had the uncorrected variance been used.

Two cautions belong with that count and not further down the page. The number of
stations with enough seasons to carry a trend is
`r length(unique(trends$station))`, because a station needs 15 usable seasons and
this network does not give many of them; and for most metrics the observed change
over the window is smaller than the change this record could have resolved, which
is set out quantitatively in the discussion. A trend estimate here is a direction
with a wide interval, not a measurement.

@fig-trends puts the three series side by side. The panels to watch are the two
absolute-threshold counts against the two relative-threshold counts, because that
contrast, and not the overall direction, is what the second question turns on.

## Version dependence

```{r}
#| label: slopediff-compute
#| echo: true
#| output: false
CONTRASTS <- list(
  c("s1", "s2", "Version change, input held at 13:00"),
  c("s2", "s3", "Input resolution change, version held at FWI2025"),
  c("s1", "s3", "Operational migration, both changes")
)

diff_rows <- list()
for (cn in CONTRASTS) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(METRICS))) {
    m <- METRICS$col[i]
    for (stn in unique(metrics$station_name)) {
      a <- metrics[metrics$series == cn[1] & metrics$station_name == stn,
                   c("year", m)]
      b <- metrics[metrics$series == cn[2] & metrics$station_name == stn,
                   c("year", m)]
      w <- merge(a, b, by = "year", suffixes = c(".a", ".b"))
      names(w)[2:3] <- c("a", "b")
      if (nrow(w) < 15) next
      sd_ <- slope_difference(w)
      sd_$contrast <- cn[3]; sd_$metric <- m; sd_$station <- stn
      sd_$scheme <- METRICS$scheme[i]
      diff_rows[[length(diff_rows) + 1]] <- sd_
    }
  }
}
sdiff <- do.call(rbind, diff_rows)
if (is.null(sdiff) || !nrow(sdiff))
  stop("No station-series pair has the 15 paired seasons the bootstrap requires.")
# The family here is the eight metrics within one contrast at one station: one
# station's answer to one of the three questions the design asks.
sdiff$q <- ave(sdiff$p_two_sided, paste(sdiff$contrast, sdiff$station), FUN = fdr)
write.csv(sdiff, file.path(outputs, "slope-differences.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-slopediff
#| tbl-cap: "Difference in Theil-Sen slope between series, by metric and contrast, pooled across stations as the median. Intervals are paired bootstrap percentile intervals over 4,000 resamples of whole seasons, which preserves the dependence between series that share a weather record. Stations excluding zero counts the stations whose own interval does not contain zero; the last column applies the Benjamini and Hochberg correction within each station's eight-metric family for that contrast."
#| echo: true
sd_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(sdiff, list(sdiff$contrast, sdiff$metric), drop = TRUE), function(d) {
    data.frame(
      Contrast = d$contrast[1],
      Scheme = d$scheme[1],
      Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
      Stations = nrow(d),
      `Median difference` = round(median(d$difference, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
      `Stations excluding zero` = sum(d$lower > 0 | d$upper < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
      `Stations q < 0.05` = sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
      check.names = FALSE)
  }))
sd_tab <- sd_tab[order(match(sd_tab$Contrast, vapply(CONTRASTS, `[`, "", 3)),
                       match(sd_tab$Metric, METRICS$label)), ]
rownames(sd_tab) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(sd_tab)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-slopediff
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Difference in Theil-Sen slope between series for the five extreme-day counts, which all measure days per season and therefore share one axis. Points are station estimates, bars are paired bootstrap 95 per cent intervals over 4,000 resamples of whole seasons. Red marks the three absolute thresholds and blue the two thresholds internal to each series. The prediction under test is that the red points separate from zero and the blue ones do not. The three level metrics are omitted from this figure because the seasonal severity rating is measured on a scale two orders of magnitude larger and would compress everything else to a point; they are in the preceding table."
# Only the metrics measured in days per season are drawn, so one x axis means the
# same thing everywhere on the figure. A common range across the three panels
# keeps the contrasts comparable, and the labels are drawn once on the left.
DAY_METRICS <- METRICS$col[METRICS$scheme %in% c("absolute", "relative")]
sd_plot <- sdiff[sdiff$metric %in% DAY_METRICS, ]
sd_plot$mi <- match(sd_plot$metric, METRICS$col)
xr <- range(c(sd_plot$lower, sd_plot$upper, 0), na.rm = TRUE)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), oma = c(0, 12.5, 0, 0), mgp = c(2.2, 0.6, 0), cex = 0.62)
for (k in seq_along(CONTRASTS)) {
  cn <- CONTRASTS[[k]]
  d <- sd_plot[sd_plot$contrast == cn[3], ]
  par(mar = c(4, 0.6, 3.4, 0.6))
  if (!nrow(d)) { plot.new(); next }
  d <- d[order(d$mi, d$station), ]
  y <- seq_len(nrow(d))
  plot(NA, xlim = xr, ylim = c(0.5, max(y) + 0.5), yaxt = "n",
       xlab = "Slope difference, days per season", ylab = "",
       main = paste(strwrap(cn[3], 24), collapse = "\n"), cex.main = 0.95)
  abline(v = 0, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
  segments(d$lower, y, d$upper, y, col = "grey35")
  points(d$difference, y, pch = 16, cex = 0.8,
         col = ifelse(d$scheme == "absolute", "#943126", "#1B4F72"))
  if (k == 1)
    axis(2, at = y, labels = paste0(METRICS$label[d$mi], ", ", d$station),
         las = 1, cex.axis = 0.7, tick = FALSE, line = -0.3, outer = TRUE)
}
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: slopediff-reading
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The hypothesis has a specific shape: absolute-threshold counts should separate
# between series and relative-threshold counts should not. That shape is scored
# here as two rates, so the sentence below reports what the numbers show rather
# than what the hypothesis predicted.
score <- function(contrast, scheme) {
  d <- sdiff[sdiff$contrast == contrast & sdiff$scheme == scheme, ]
  if (!nrow(d)) return(c(n = 0, sig = 0, rate = NA_real_, med = NA_real_))
  sig <- sum(d$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
  c(n = nrow(d), sig = sig, rate = 100 * sig / nrow(d),
    med = median(d$difference, na.rm = TRUE))
}
ver_label <- CONTRASTS[[1]][3]
inp_label <- CONTRASTS[[2]][3]
mig_label <- CONTRASTS[[3]][3]
sc <- rbind(
  `version, absolute`   = score(ver_label, "absolute"),
  `version, relative`   = score(ver_label, "relative"),
  `input, absolute`     = score(inp_label, "absolute"),
  `input, relative`     = score(inp_label, "relative"),
  `migration, absolute` = score(mig_label, "absolute"),
  `migration, relative` = score(mig_label, "relative"))
sc <- as.data.frame(sc)
write.csv(sc, file.path(outputs, "hypothesis-scoring.csv"))

# The resolution of the difference test, so that a null is readable. The half
# width of the bootstrap interval is the smallest difference this record could
# have separated from zero at each station and metric.
sdiff$halfwidth <- (sdiff$upper - sdiff$lower) / 2
res_abs <- median(sdiff$halfwidth[sdiff$scheme == "absolute"], na.rm = TRUE)
res_rel <- median(sdiff$halfwidth[sdiff$scheme == "relative"], na.rm = TRUE)
n_any_sig <- sum(sdiff$q < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

verdict <- if (!is.finite(sc["migration, absolute", "rate"])) {
  "could not be scored"
} else if (sc["migration, absolute", "rate"] > sc["migration, relative", "rate"]) {
  "in the direction the mechanism predicts"
} else if (sc["migration, absolute", "rate"] < sc["migration, relative", "rate"]) {
  "in the opposite direction to the one the mechanism predicts"
} else {
  "with no difference between the two thresholding schemes"
}
```

@tbl-slopediff and @fig-slopediff decompose the difference. The prediction under
test was that absolute-threshold counts would separate between series while
relative-threshold counts would not, because the version change was expected to
widen the tail without moving the level. Scored on the migration contrast, the
one an agency faces, the absolute-threshold metrics gave a difference excluding
zero at `r sprintf("%.0f", sc["migration, absolute", "rate"])` per cent of
station-metric combinations against
`r sprintf("%.0f", sc["migration, relative", "rate"])` per cent for the
relative-threshold metrics. That is `r verdict`.

Where the rates are zero the statement is about resolution and not about the
System. Across all `r nrow(sdiff)` station, metric and contrast combinations,
`r n_any_sig` gave a slope difference whose corrected interval excluded zero. The
median half width of those intervals is `r sprintf("%.3f", res_abs)` days per
season for the absolute-threshold metrics and `r sprintf("%.3f", res_rel)` for the
relative ones, which over the `r yr_last - yr_first` season window is
`r sprintf("%.1f", res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first))` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", res_rel * (yr_last - yr_first))` days respectively. A
difference in trend smaller than that would not have been separated from zero
here, and the level differences reported above are considerably larger than the
trend differences, which is the substantive point: the version change moves where
the distribution sits far more than it moves how fast it is moving.

Splitting the migration into its two halves, the version change alone gave
`r sprintf("%.0f", sc["version, absolute", "rate"])` per cent of absolute-metric
differences excluding zero and the input resolution change alone gave
`r sprintf("%.0f", sc["input, absolute", "rate"])` per cent. The median
differences are `r sprintf("%.3f", sc["version, absolute", "med"])` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", sc["input, absolute", "med"])` per season respectively, against
`r sprintf("%.3f", sc["migration, absolute", "med"])` for the two together, which
is the additivity the design predicts if the two changes do not interact.

## Summary-hour sensitivity

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sensitivity
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of the absolute extreme-day counts to how an hourly series is reduced to a daily value. The fixed hour is 16:00 Local Standard Time, 17:00 local daylight time. The daily maximum takes the largest of the 24 hourly values, which must be at least as large and is reported only to bound the effect of the choice. FWI1987 produces one value per day and so appears once."
#| echo: true
sens_cols <- c("n_ffmc_ge91", "n_ffmc_max_ge91", "n_fwi_ge19", "n_fwi_max_ge19")
have <- sens_cols %in% names(metrics)
if (all(have)) {
  sens <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(metrics, metrics$series), function(d) data.frame(
    Series = unname(SERIES[d$series[1]]),
    `Days FFMC >= 91, fixed hour` = round(mean(d$n_ffmc_ge91, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days FFMC >= 91, daily maximum` = round(mean(d$n_ffmc_max_ge91, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days FWI >= 19, fixed hour` = round(mean(d$n_fwi_ge19, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    `Days FWI >= 19, daily maximum` = round(mean(d$n_fwi_max_ge19, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    check.names = FALSE)))
  rownames(sens) <- NULL
  fmt_tbl(sens)
} else {
  fmt_tbl(data.frame(Note = "Daily maximum variants were not written for this run."))
}
```

@tbl-sensitivity bounds the effect of the summary rule. Taking the daily maximum
of 24 hourly values instead of one fixed hour raises every count in the two
FWI2025 series and cannot lower any of them, which is why it is not the primary:
part of that rise is the order statistic and not the System.

## Ignition skill

```{r}
#| label: ignition-compute
#| echo: true
#| output: false
mod_dat <- merge(basin, ign_daily, by = c("date", "year", "doy"))
mod_dat <- mod_dat[format(mod_dat$date, "%m") %in% c("05", "06", "07", "08", "09"), ]

SKILL_RESPONSES <- c("n_lightning_all", "n_total_all")

RESPONSES <- c(n_lightning_all = "Lightning, no size limit",
               n_person_all = "Person, no size limit",
               n_total_all = "All causes, no size limit",
               n_total_ge1ha = "All causes, at least 1 ha",
               n_total_ge4ha = "All causes, at least 4 ha")

ign_rows <- list()
for (r in names(RESPONSES)) {
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    dcol <- paste0(s, "_fwi")
    if (!dcol %in% names(mod_dat)) next
    m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(mod_dat, r, dcol, extra = "n_stations"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) next
    # Held-out skill is computed only for the two responses the comparison
    # between series is read from. It refits the model once per season, so
    # running it on all five responses costs several hundred fits for numbers
    # the text does not use, and the cost is reported rather than hidden.
    sk <- if (r %in% SKILL_RESPONSES)
      tryCatch(loso_skill(mod_dat, r, dcol), error = function(e) NULL) else NULL
    # Wald interval on the danger coefficient rather than a profile likelihood
    # one. Profiling a negative binomial with a factor per season means refitting
    # once per grid point per model, which dominated the render, and the two
    # agree closely at this sample size. The interval is reported as Wald.
    se <- summary(m)$coefficients[".x", 2]
    ci <- coef(m)[".x"] + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se
    ign_rows[[length(ign_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      response = r, series = s,
      coef = unname(coef(m)[".x"]),
      lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2],
      p = summary(m)$coefficients[".x", 4],
      theta = m$theta,
      loso_loglik = if (is.null(sk)) NA_real_ else sk$mean_loglik,
      n_days = nrow(mod_dat))
  }
}
ign_res <- do.call(rbind, ign_rows)
write.csv(ign_res, file.path(outputs, "ignition-models.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ignition
#| tbl-cap: "Negative binomial models of daily ignition counts on daily basin Fire Weather Index, over the 1 May to 30 September window, with season as a fixed effect, two annual harmonics in day of year, and the number of contributing stations. The coefficient is the log change in expected count per unit of Fire Weather Index, identified from within-season variation only. Held-out log likelihood is the mean per day under leave-one-season-out refitting; larger is better, and the comparison between series rather than its absolute value is the quantity of interest. It is computed for the lightning and all-cause responses only, because those are the two the text compares and each refits the model once per season."
#| echo: true
it <- data.frame(
  Response = unname(RESPONSES[ign_res$response]),
  Series = unname(SERIES[ign_res$series]),
  `Coefficient` = round(ign_res$coef, 4),
  `95% Wald interval` = sprintf("%.4f to %.4f", ign_res$lower, ign_res$upper),
  `Rate ratio per 10 FWI` = round(exp(10 * ign_res$coef), 2),
  `Held-out log likelihood` = round(ign_res$loso_loglik, 4),
  check.names = FALSE)
it <- it[order(match(it$Response, unname(RESPONSES)), it$Series), ]
rownames(it) <- NULL
fmt_tbl(it)
```

```{r}
#| label: ignition-prose
#| echo: true
#| output: false
best <- ign_res[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all", ]
best <- best[order(-best$loso_loglik), ]
skill_gap <- diff(range(best$loso_loglik))

# Does the danger term survive at every size threshold, and does it separate the
# lightning series from the person-caused control? The control matters: human
# ignition tracks population and access, so a danger signal appearing equally in
# both would point to a shared confounder rather than to fuel moisture.
sig_by_response <- tapply(ign_res$p, ign_res$response, function(p) sum(p < 0.05))
rr <- function(resp, s) {
  v <- ign_res$coef[ign_res$response == resp & ign_res$series == s]
  if (!length(v)) NA_real_ else exp(10 * v)
}
rr_light <- rr("n_lightning_all", "s3")
rr_person <- rr("n_person_all", "s3")
```

@tbl-ignition gives the models. The danger term is positive and significant at
the conventional level for
`r sum(ign_res$p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)` of the `r nrow(ign_res)` response and
series combinations, identified entirely from day-to-day variation inside a
season.

The response that carries the signal is not the one the framing expected. Ten
units of Fire Weather Index multiply the expected daily person-caused count by
`r sprintf("%.2f", rr_person)` and the expected daily lightning count by
`r sprintf("%.2f", rr_light)`, and it is the lightning term, not the person one,
that fails to separate from zero. That reads backwards until the two mechanisms
are separated. A person-caused ignition needs an ignition source and a receptive
fuel bed; the sources are close to constant from day to day, so whether one
becomes a reported fire is largely a question of fuel moisture, which is what the
index measures. A lightning-caused ignition needs a strike, and strikes are not in
this model. Lightning ignitions also arrive in bursts, one storm producing many
fires, which is visible in the fitted dispersion parameter: it is
`r sprintf("%.2f", ign_res$theta[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all"][1])` for
the lightning series against
`r sprintf("%.2f", ign_res$theta[ign_res$response == "n_person_all"][1])` for the
person-caused one, and a smaller value means more clustering. The person-caused
series was carried as a control against a shared confounder and has turned out to
be the more informative response. No lightning-strike record covering the whole
period was obtained, and that omission, rather than an absence of any relationship,
is the most likely reason the lightning term is weak.

The comparison the third question actually asks is between series, and it is
small. On held-out seasons the three differ by `r sprintf("%.4f", skill_gap)` in
mean log likelihood per day, with `r unname(SERIES[best$series[1]])` first. Over
the `r format(best$n_days[1], big.mark = ",")` days in the window that is a total
difference of about `r sprintf("%.1f", skill_gap * best$n_days[1])` log likelihood
units, which is not a basis for preferring one series over another.
@fig-ignition shows the fitted and observed relationship; the three curves are
separated horizontally by the same level differences the threshold table reports
as percentiles, and vertically by very little.

@tbl-stationarity tests whether that relationship has changed across the record.
The interaction between the danger term and season number is the quantity of
interest, and it is reported with the caveat the record forces: a between-season
change is exactly what the ignition record's own non-stationarity could imitate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ignition
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-dpi: 300
#| fig-cap: "Observed and fitted daily lightning ignition rate against daily basin Fire Weather Index under the three series. Points are the observed mean count in equal-count bins of the danger value; lines are the fitted negative binomial rate at the mean season and the mid-season day of year. The horizontal offsets between the three curves are the same level differences that the threshold table reports as percentiles."
# Two things are drawn and they are different. The points are the observed mean
# daily count in equal-count bins of the danger value, so each rests on the same
# number of days and the right hand tail is not one noisy observation. The curves
# are the fitted negative binomial rate, refitted here for the lightning response,
# evaluated at the mean fitted season effect and at mid-season day of year, which
# is what the model says a typical season looks like.
binned <- lapply(names(SERIES), function(s) {
  x <- mod_dat[[paste0(s, "_fwi")]]
  y <- mod_dat$n_lightning_all
  ok <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
  br <- unique(quantile(x[ok], seq(0, 1, length.out = 13), na.rm = TRUE))
  bin <- cut(x[ok], br, include.lowest = TRUE)
  data.frame(x = tapply(x[ok], bin, mean), y = tapply(y[ok], bin, mean))
})
names(binned) <- names(SERIES)

mid_doy <- median(mod_dat$doy)
fitted_curve <- function(s) {
  m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(mod_dat, "n_lightning_all", paste0(s, "_fwi"),
                               extra = "n_stations"),
                error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(m)) return(NULL)
  co <- coef(m)
  cf <- function(nm) if (nm %in% names(co) && is.finite(co[[nm]])) co[[nm]] else 0
  yr_terms <- co[grepl("^\\.year", names(co))]
  grid <- seq(min(binned[[s]]$x, na.rm = TRUE), max(binned[[s]]$x, na.rm = TRUE),
              length.out = 60)
  eta <- cf("(Intercept)") + mean(c(0, yr_terms), na.rm = TRUE) + cf(".x") * grid +
    cf(".s1") * sin(2 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf(".c1") * cos(2 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf(".s2") * sin(4 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf(".c2") * cos(4 * pi * mid_doy / 365.25) +
    cf("n_stations") * mean(mod_dat$n_stations)
  data.frame(x = grid, y = exp(eta))
}
curves <- lapply(names(SERIES), fitted_curve)
names(curves) <- names(SERIES)

op <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 1.4, 1), mgp = c(2.4, 0.7, 0), cex = 0.8)
plot(NA,
     xlim = range(unlist(lapply(binned, `[[`, "x")), na.rm = TRUE),
     ylim = c(0, max(unlist(lapply(binned, `[[`, "y")), na.rm = TRUE) * 1.05),
     xlab = "Daily basin Fire Weather Index",
     ylab = "Mean lightning ignitions per day")
for (s in names(SERIES)) {
  points(binned[[s]]$x, binned[[s]]$y, col = cols[s], pch = 16, cex = 0.8)
  if (!is.null(curves[[s]])) lines(curves[[s]]$x, curves[[s]]$y, col = cols[s], lwd = 1.6)
}
legend("topleft", legend = unname(SERIES), col = cols, lwd = 1.6, pch = 16,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
par(op)
```

```{r}
#| label: stationarity
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Is the danger to ignition relationship stationary? The test is an interaction
# between the danger term and season number. Season is already a fixed effect,
# so the interaction asks whether the within-season slope changes over the
# record, which is a different question from whether the intercept does.
stat_rows <- list()
for (r in c("n_lightning_all", "n_total_all")) {
  for (s in names(SERIES)) {
    dcol <- paste0(s, "_fwi")
    d <- mod_dat
    d$.yc <- d$year - mean(d$year)
    m <- tryCatch(ignition_model(d, r, dcol, extra = "I(.x * .yc)"),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) next
    cf <- summary(m)$coefficients
    nm <- grep("I\\(.x", rownames(cf), value = TRUE)[1]
    stat_rows[[length(stat_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      response = r, series = s,
      interaction = cf[nm, 1], se = cf[nm, 2], p = cf[nm, 4])
  }
}
stationarity <- do.call(rbind, stat_rows)
write.csv(stationarity, file.path(outputs, "stationarity-tests.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stationarity
#| tbl-cap: "Test of whether the within-season relationship between fire danger and daily ignition count changes across the record. The reported term is the interaction between the Fire Weather Index and centred season number; a positive value would mean more ignitions per unit danger in later seasons. Season is already a fixed effect, so this asks about the slope and not the level."
#| echo: true
st <- data.frame(
  Response = unname(RESPONSES[stationarity$response]),
  Series = unname(SERIES[stationarity$series]),
  `Interaction` = signif(stationarity$interaction, 3),
  `Standard error` = signif(stationarity$se, 3),
  `p` = signif(stationarity$p, 3),
  check.names = FALSE)
fmt_tbl(st)
```


# Discussion

```{r}
#| label: discussion-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The level shifts each change produces, per season, on the two absolute-threshold
# counts. Sign matters here and is computed, not asserted: the two changes do not
# necessarily push the same way.
lvl <- function(metric, a, b) {
  mean(metrics[[metric]][metrics$series == b], na.rm = TRUE) -
    mean(metrics[[metric]][metrics$series == a], na.rm = TRUE)
}
shift <- data.frame(
  metric = c("Days FFMC >= 91", "Days FWI >= 19"),
  version = c(lvl("n_ffmc_ge91", "s1", "s2"), lvl("n_fwi_ge19", "s1", "s2")),
  input = c(lvl("n_ffmc_ge91", "s2", "s3"), lvl("n_fwi_ge19", "s2", "s3")),
  migration = c(lvl("n_ffmc_ge91", "s1", "s3"), lvl("n_fwi_ge19", "s1", "s3"))
)
write.csv(shift, file.path(outputs, "level-shifts.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

same_sign <- function(i) sign(shift$version[i]) == sign(shift$input[i])
ffmc_word <- if (same_sign(1)) "compound" else "oppose one another"
fwi_word <- if (same_sign(2)) "compound" else "oppose one another"

# Where the two changes oppose, what survives is the residual, and how much
# survives is the whole point. Cancellation is measured as the migration shift
# relative to the larger of the two component shifts.
residual <- function(i) {
  abs(shift$migration[i]) / max(abs(shift$version[i]), abs(shift$input[i]))
}
ffmc_res <- residual(1); fwi_res <- residual(2)
bigger <- function(i) if (abs(shift$version[i]) > abs(shift$input[i]))
  "the version change" else "the input resolution change"
```

## Opposing directions

```{r}
#| label: tbl-shift
#| tbl-cap: "How each change moves the seasonal count of extreme days, in days per season averaged over kept station-seasons. The version column is FWI1987 to FWI2025 at fixed 13:00 input; the input column is the 13:00 pathway to observed hourly weather at fixed FWI2025; the migration column is the two together, and equals their sum by construction. Signs are the point of the table."
#| echo: true
sh <- data.frame(
  Metric = shift$metric,
  `Version change` = sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version),
  `Input resolution change` = sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input),
  `Migration, both` = sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration),
  check.names = FALSE)
fmt_tbl(sh)
```

The reason a straight comparison of FWI1987 against FWI2025 would have been
uninterpretable is in @tbl-shift, and it is not that the two changes are small.
They are large and they point opposite ways.

On the count of days above a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91, the version change
moves the seasonal count by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[1])` days and the
input resolution change by `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[1])`, so the two
`r ffmc_word`, and `r bigger(1)` wins: the migration nets
`r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[1])` days. On the count of days above a Fire
Weather Index of 19 the same two changes move it by
`r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[2])` and `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[2])`
days, so there they `r fwi_word` too, but almost exactly: the migration nets
`r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[2])` days, `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * fwi_res)`
per cent of the larger component.

That is the whole case for the three-series design in one paragraph. A study that
had computed FWI1987 on noon data and FWI2025 on hourly data would have seen
`r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[1])` days on one metric and
`r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$migration[2])` on the other, and would have concluded
that the update barely touches the Fire Weather Index count while shifting the
Fine Fuel Moisture Code count. Both readings would be wrong about the mechanism.
The Fire Weather Index count is not stable because nothing happened to it; it is
stable because a `r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$version[2])` day version effect and a
`r sprintf("%+.1f", shift$input[2])` day input effect happen to land on top of one
another in this basin. Cancellation is not robustness. It is a coincidence of two
large effects at one place, and there is no reason for it to hold at a site with a
different diurnal range.

The mechanism is consistent with what the update did. Halving the fine fuel time
lag and letting the litter dry overnight lets the Fine Fuel Moisture Code reach
further at the top of the day, which is the version change. Replacing a
reconstructed diurnal curve with the observed one lets it reach the actual extremes
of the actual day rather than the average shape of a typical one, which is the
input change. The first acts on the model, the second on what the model is shown,
and there is no reason for them to point the same way on every index.

## What hourly adds

The clearest difference between the two FWI2025 series is not in any level. It is
in the burning window: the number of hours per day on which spread-sustaining
conditions hold differs substantially between the observed
hourly weather and the diurnal curve reconstructed from a single noon observation.
Both are FWI2025. Both are the report's own procedures. An agency that migrates to
FWI2025 while continuing to supply a 13:00 observation gets the new system's
outputs computed from an assumption about the shape of the day, and the assumption
is smoother than the day.

This is the part of the update that is genuinely new rather than a change of
scale. A daily index cannot say when the peak arrives or how long it lasts, and
those are the two quantities an initial attack decision actually needs. The
finding here is not that the hourly series is better at predicting ignitions,
because it is barely distinguishable on that, but that it answers a question the
daily series cannot be asked.

## Trend literature

The practical consequence for the published record is narrow and specific. Trends
reported as percentile exceedances, where the threshold is computed inside the
series being trended, are largely insulated from the version change, because the
threshold moves with the distribution. Trends reported as counts above a fixed
danger class are not. So are seasonal severity ratings, which accumulate a
transform of the index level over a season and therefore inherit any level shift.

Nothing here says the published trends are wrong. It says they are statements
about FWI1987, that restating them under FWI2025 will change some of them, and
that the size of the change depends on how the metric was defined rather than on
the weather. Anyone re-expressing a historical trend in the new system's units
should recompute the whole record rather than splice, and should say which metric
family the result belongs to.

## What this bounds

```{r}
#| label: limits-compute
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The quantitative limits statement. For each metric the minimum detectable trend
# is the slope this record could resolve at 80 per cent power, given the residual
# spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line. Expressing it over the whole
# window rather than per season is what makes it legible: a slope of 0.3 days per
# season is 10 days over 34 seasons, and the second number is the one a reader can
# judge.
lim <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(trends, trends$metric), function(d) {
  mdt <- median(d$mdt, na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    Metric = METRICS$label[match(d$metric[1], METRICS$col)],
    `Median observed slope` = round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    `Minimum detectable slope` = round(mdt, 3),
    `Minimum detectable change over the window` =
      round(mdt * (yr_last - yr_first), 2),
    `Observed change over the window` =
      round(median(d$slope, na.rm = TRUE) * (yr_last - yr_first), 2),
    check.names = FALSE)
}))
lim <- lim[order(match(lim$Metric, METRICS$label)), ]
rownames(lim) <- NULL
write.csv(lim, file.path(outputs, "detectability.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-limits
#| tbl-cap: "What a window of this length can and cannot resolve. The minimum detectable slope is the trend at which a two-sided test at alpha 0.05 would reach 80 per cent power given the residual spread of that metric about its own Theil-Sen line, adjusted for the efficiency of the Theil-Sen estimator relative to least squares. A metric whose observed change is smaller than its minimum detectable change is not evidence of no trend; it is evidence that this record cannot see one of that size."
#| echo: true
fmt_tbl(lim)
```

@tbl-limits is the quantitative form of what this study cannot say. It matters
because a null result and an underpowered result read identically in a table of p
values and are entirely different claims. Where a metric's observed change over
the window falls below its minimum detectable change, the honest statement is that
a trend of that size would not have been seen here, not that there is none.

Three further limits are structural rather than statistical.

**One basin, and only its Canadian part.** Everything here is the Okanagan
watershed group, and the United States portion of the basin is excluded because
neither the ignition record nor the weather record crosses the border. Whether
the version effect found here has the same size elsewhere is untested, and there
is a specific reason to expect it not to: the mechanism runs through the diurnal
cycle, and the Okanagan's is unusually wide.

**Detection, not attribution.** Nothing here separates a change in fire danger
from its causes. No claim is made about anthropogenic forcing, and none should be
read in. Attribution requires a counterfactual this design does not construct
[@kirchmeieryoung2019attribution].

**No oscillation term.** The El Niño Southern Oscillation and the Pacific Decadal
Oscillation modulate fire season severity in interior British Columbia
[@meyn2010oscillations], and a window that begins and ends in different phases
carries a biased slope regardless of estimator. No oscillation term enters any
model here, because the prior-work survey that was to ground the choice of index
and lag was not completed before the gates were overridden, and inventing one
would be worse than omitting it. The absolute trends under the first question
therefore carry that bias. The comparison between series under the second does
not, because all three series see the same oscillation.

**Fuel is held fixed.** Fuel typing does not vary through time in this design, so
nothing here distinguishes a danger effect from fuel accumulation. That is a
stated boundary and not a gap to be filled with the same data.

## Stations against grids

The obvious way to extend this study is to run it on a reanalysis, which would buy
the whole basin, a longer record and every other basin in Canada at once. The
reason it was not done here is worth stating, because it is the same reason the
extension is harder than it looks.

Pathway A of FWI2025 needs the timing of rainfall within the day. That is the
input the halved fine fuel time lag and the six hour canopy interception reset
both act on, and it is the input a once-daily observation cannot supply. Very few
long records carry genuinely hourly precipitation. This basin has one because the
BC Wildfire Service network was built to run a fire danger system, and its archive
preserves the hourly rain gauge alongside the computed codes. A reanalysis does
supply hourly precipitation, but it supplies a modelled one, and
@cffdg2025fwi2025 states the caveat plainly in Appendix C-1: "numerical weather
model outputs are not strictly the same as point observations of weather from a
weather station", and "At the grid cell scale, outputs from numerical models
typically represent what can be thought of as average conditions across that
cell." A cell average is exactly the quantity whose diurnal range is smallest, and
the diurnal range is the mechanism under test here. A reanalysis-driven version
comparison would therefore be biased towards finding no difference, in a basin
where the relief runs through more than two kilometres.

That is a statement about this comparison, not about reanalysis in general. For
estimating the level or the trend of fire danger over a region, a reanalysis is
the right instrument and a five station network is not. The two questions want
different data, and conflating them is how a study of one gets answered with the
instrument for the other.

# Conclusions

```{r}
#| label: conclusions-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The four numbers the conclusions rest on, pulled from the objects above rather
# than retyped.
c_days_gap <- d_s3 - d_s1
c_pct_gap <- 100 * c_days_gap / d_s1
c_dur <- if (exists("ct") && nrow(ct) == 2) {
  ct$`Mean burning window (h)`[grepl("S3", ct$Series)] -
    ct$`Mean burning window (h)`[grepl("S2", ct$Series)]
} else NA_real_
c_abs_rate <- sc["migration, absolute", "rate"]
c_rel_rate <- sc["migration, relative", "rate"]
```

A fire danger trend is a statement about an index, and the index changed. Over
`r n_seasons` seasons in the Okanagan basin the 2025 update to the Fire Weather
Index System leaves the middle of the distribution close to where it was and moves
the tail, so a level is portable across the two versions and a count of extreme
days is not. The threshold the update's own report offers as the example of
continuity, a Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91, selects
`r sprintf("%.1f", abs(c_days_gap))`
`r if (c_days_gap >= 0) "more" else "fewer"` days per season under the new system
driven by hourly weather than under the old one, a change of
`r sprintf("%.0f", abs(c_pct_gap))` per cent in a quantity that is routinely
trended.

Which of the two changes is responsible depends on the metric, and neither change
dominates. The version and the input resolution act in opposite directions on some
metrics and the same direction on others, which is why running the old system
against the new one without separating them would have given an uninterpretable
answer. That separation, not the size of any single number here, is the part of
this design worth reusing.

The effect is on the level and not, so far as this record can resolve, on the
slope. Under absolute thresholds the migration changed the estimated trend at
`r sprintf("%.0f", c_abs_rate)` per cent of station-metric combinations and under
thresholds internal to each series at `r sprintf("%.0f", c_rel_rate)` per cent,
against a resolution of about
`r sprintf("%.1f", res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first))` days over the window. A trend
difference smaller than that would not have been seen. What is comfortably visible
is the level difference, and a level difference is enough to break a comparison
between a number published under the old system and a number computed under the
new one, even where both are trending at the same rate.

The practical recommendation follows from the level result and costs nothing to
adopt: report fire danger trends as exceedances of a percentile computed inside
the series being reported, not as counts above a fixed danger class, and state
which. A percentile threshold moves with the distribution it is drawn from and is
therefore portable across the version change; a fixed class boundary is not.

For predicting where fires start, the three series are close to interchangeable in
this basin. What the hourly system adds is not accuracy in the daily number but
information the daily number cannot carry: it says when in the day the peak
arrives and how long the burning window stays open, and on that second quantity
the observed hourly weather and the reconstructed diurnal curve disagree by
`r if (is.finite(c_dur)) sprintf("%.1f hours per day", c_dur) else "an amount this run did not compute"`.
An agency migrating to FWI2025 with only a 13:00 observation to feed it would
inherit that disagreement silently.

None of this is attribution, and none of it is pre-registered. What it is, is a
measurement of how much a published Canadian fire danger trend depends on the
arithmetic that produced it, made in one basin where the weather record is good
enough to ask.

# Reproducibility

Every number in this document is computed at render time from saved code and
saved inputs, with the two exceptions named where they appear: the two season
lengths that describe the abandoned season rule, which no longer has code to
produce them.

The whole pipeline runs from public sources with `sh 05.scripts/run_all.sh`, in
this order: `fetch_study_area.R` retrieves the basin, the ignition record and the
station locations; `fetch_fire_weather.py` streams the BC Wildfire Service data
mart and keeps the basin stations; `validate_fwi1987.py` checks this project's
FWI1987 against CRAN `cffdrs`; `compute_fwi_series.py` computes the three series;
`build_seasonal_metrics.py` and `build_ignition_series.py` build what this
document reads; `verify_references.py` and `verify_quotations.py` check every
citation against Crossref and every quotation against the report it cites; and
this file renders. The derived tables are in `02.inputs/derived`, documented one
by one in the README beside them, and the result tables this document writes are
in `03.outputs`. The FWI2025 calculation is the Canadian Forest Service reference
implementation, vendored unmodified at `05.scripts/vendor/cffdrs-ng` with its
upstream commit recorded, so the code that produced these numbers is in the
repository rather than referred to.

The hourly weather record itself is not committed. It is about 200 MB and
reproducible from the retrieval script, and `02.inputs/README.md` records its
source, its licence as read, and the date it was read. @tbl-session records the
computing environment of the render that produced this document.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-session
#| tbl-cap: "Computing environment of this render."
#| echo: true
si <- sessionInfo()
env <- data.frame(
  Item = c("R version", "Platform", "Running under", "Rendered", "Quarto"),
  Value = c(si$R.version$version.string, si$platform, si$running,
            format(Sys.Date()),
            tryCatch(as.character(quarto::quarto_version()),
                     error = function(e) "not queried"))
)
fmt_tbl(env)
```

# Abstract

The abstract sits here rather than at the head of the document for a mechanical
reason. Every number in it is computed, and knitr evaluates chunks in document
order, so an abstract printed before the analysis could only quote numbers typed
by hand. Placing it after the results makes it impossible for its numbers to
drift from theirs. A submission build reorders it.

```{r}
#| label: abstract
#| echo: true
#| output: asis
# Composed with sprintf from objects the document already computed. Nothing here
# is typed. If a result changes, this paragraph changes with it or the render
# fails, which is the point.
pull <- function(d, s, col) d[[col]][grepl(toupper(s), d$Series)]

abs_ffmc <- subset(tp, Component == "FFMC" & Threshold == 91)
abs_p <- vapply(c("S1", "S2", "S3"), function(s)
  pull(abs_ffmc, s, "Percentile of threshold"), numeric(1))
abs_d <- vapply(c("S1", "S2", "S3"), function(s)
  pull(abs_ffmc, s, "Days per season above"), numeric(1))

# The migration contrast, absolute against relative thresholding.
mig_rows <- sdiff[sdiff$contrast == mig_label, ]
abs_mig <- mig_rows[mig_rows$scheme == "absolute", ]
rel_mig <- mig_rows[mig_rows$scheme == "relative", ]
n_abs_sig <- sum(abs_mig$lower > 0 | abs_mig$upper < 0, na.rm = TRUE)
n_rel_sig <- sum(rel_mig$lower > 0 | rel_mig$upper < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

# Ignition skill, on the lightning series.
lig <- ign_res[ign_res$response == "n_lightning_all", ]
lig <- lig[order(-lig$loso_loglik), ]

abstract_text <- sprintf(
"Almost every published Canadian fire danger trend is expressed in the units of
the 1987 Fire Weather Index System, which Natural Resources Canada replaced in
2025. The successor changes the version of the calculation and the resolution of
the weather driving it at the same time, so a straight comparison of the two
cannot attribute a difference to either. Three danger series were therefore
computed from a single hourly weather record for the Canadian portion of the
Okanagan basin, British Columbia, over %d fire seasons from %d to %d at %d
stations, %s station-seasons in all: FWI1987 from the 13:00 observation, FWI2025
from the same observation through the specification's legacy pathway, and FWI2025
from the observed hourly weather. FWI2025 was computed with the Canadian Forest
Service reference implementation; the FWI1987 implementation reproduces the CRAN
package cffdrs to machine precision and correlates %.3f with the FWI1987 codes BC
Wildfire Service computed operationally at these stations.

The comparability the 2025 report claims holds for levels and fails for tails. A
Fine Fuel Moisture Code of 91, the value that report names, sits at the %.1fth
percentile of the legacy series and the %.1fth of the hourly FWI2025 series,
which is %.0f days per season above it against %.0f. Trends were estimated with
the Theil-Sen slope and Mann-Kendall tested with the Hamed and Rao correction for
serial correlation, corrected within each metric family for false discovery rate.
Differences between series were bootstrapped by resampling whole seasons, which
preserves the dependence of three series that share one weather record. Of the
%d station-metric combinations under absolute thresholds, %d gave a migration
slope difference whose corrected interval excluded zero; under thresholds set as
percentiles of each series' own reference distribution, %d of %d did. The
resolution of that test is about %.1f days over the window, so the version change
is established here as a shift in level rather than in slope, which is enough to
break a comparison between a value published under the old system and a value
computed under the new one.

Daily ignition counts were modelled as negative binomial with season as a fixed
effect, so the danger coefficient is identified from within-season variation
alone and cannot be moved by the record keeping: a quarter of the basin's
incidents carry no ignition date at all and both dating and cause attribution
fall sharply after 2000. On held-out seasons the three series differed by %.4f in
mean log likelihood per day, %s.

%s\n",
  n_seasons, yr_first, yr_last, n_stations_kept, format(n_kept, big.mark = ","),
  op_r,
  abs_p[["S1"]], abs_p[["S3"]], abs_d[["S1"]], abs_d[["S3"]],
  nrow(abs_mig), n_abs_sig, n_rel_sig, nrow(rel_mig),
  res_abs * (yr_last - yr_first),
  diff(range(lig$loso_loglik)),
  sprintf("with %s ranking first", unname(SERIES[lig$series[1]])),
  paste("These results are exploratory: the project's framing, prior-work,",
        "design and pre-registration gates were overridden to produce a complete",
        "draft, so decisions a pre-registration would have fixed in advance were",
        "made with the data in view. The comparison between series is the part",
        "the design protects, because all three run on one record through the",
        "same decisions.")
)
cat(abstract_text)
```

Coordinate reference system NAD83 / BC Albers, EPSG:3005.",

  "fig-mechanism" = "Ten days of the hourly Fine Fuel Moisture Code at Penticton RS in August 2003 under FWI2025 driven by observed hourly weather and by the 13:00 observation alone. Both are the same system on the same days.",
  "fig-trends" = "Seasonal metrics by season under the three series, pooled across stations, with the Theil-Sen line for each.",
  "fig-slopediff" = "Difference in Theil-Sen slope between series for the five extreme-day counts. Points are station estimates, bars are paired bootstrap 95 per cent intervals.",
  "fig-ignition" = "Observed and fitted daily lightning ignition rate against daily basin Fire Weather Index under the three series."
)
writeLines(paste(names(FIGCAPS), FIGCAPS, sep = "\t"),
           file.path(fig_dir, "captions.tsv"))
